A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from GLOS to SIGNER, and their supplied text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. Neither includes a substantive appendix. However, v2 explicitly refers to supplementary evaluator details and cross-evaluator results that are absent from the supplied file, limiting comparison of those components.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark experiments, conditioning and attention ablations, robustness tests, and qualitative generation results on CSL-Daily and PHOENIX-2014T.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, revised ablations and robustness experiments, qualitative comparisons, and new motion-smoothness measurements in Table 5 and Figure 6.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 replaces training-set gloss-length statistics and an unseen-gloss fallback with an MLP that predicts durations from gloss embeddings. Section 4.3 and Figure 4 expand IPA from body-hand interactions to include face-body interactions. These change generation and feature exchange; renaming TAC to LTF largely preserves the AdaLN-plus-convolution fusion mechanism.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Chinese and German text-to-sign generation on CSL-Daily and PHOENIX-2014T. The added smoothness analysis and revised gloss/duration controls concern the retained coverage; no additional dataset, language, population, or task is evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds G2P-DDM and NAT-EA and removes T2S-GPT. NAT-EA joins the opening qualitative comparison and replaces NSA in the later qualitative figure. Spoken2Sign becomes an evaluated comparator in the new smoothness study, alongside NSA, MoMask, and NAT-EA.

E3.justification: v1 describes a resource-constrained reimplementation of the back-translation encoder; v2 reports retraining all methods with a common face-inclusive representation and matching evaluator. Test-length ablations and train/test-length main results give way to estimated-duration results with a test-duration control. v2 also introduces peak-velocity/jerk metrics and random duration perturbations. The revised settings prevent direct cross-version performance comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds motion-smoothness measurements and two jerk-curve case studies, a ground-truth-gloss control, random duration perturbations, and the previously missing face-only IPA configuration. It removes the pooled-text and pooled-gloss controls from Table 1 and the +8 duration perturbation. Qualitative examples and comparators are also revised.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates only. v2 Table 5 introduces ± statistics for peak velocity and jerk, but does not define their meaning or report repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals. This establishes changed variability reporting, not an increase in experimental runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 extensively replace numerical results under revised settings. Table 2 reverses the face-attention ranking: v1 favors excluding face attention, with BLEU-4 13.27 versus 12.79; v2 favors full IPA, with 15.60 versus 13.59 without face attention. New Table 5 reports SIGNER peak velocity 0.38±0.10 and peak jerk 0.35±0.12. These are not same-setting cross-version gains.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.3 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the diffusion loss as expected original-token negative log-likelihood, whereas v1 only references variational lower-bound training. The existing VQ-VAE and diffusion-transition equations are retained. No theorem, proof, or formal guarantee is added.

C1.justification: The central claims of improved lexical order, semantic accuracy, and state-of-the-art performance on the same two datasets remain. v2 refines the contribution emphasis toward LTF and temporal grounding, broadening the criticized mechanism from sentence-level conditioning to global fusion even when gloss conditions are available.

C2.justification: v1 explains face attention as potentially redundant or noisy because facial expressions lack diversity; v2 instead interprets facial cues as complementary and supports full IPA. v2 also interprets comparisons with NAT-EA as evidence that temporal-gloss conditions alone are insufficient, adds smoothness-based interpretations, and explicitly identifies the need for a text-to-gloss model when transferring to another language.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 529-dimensional motion representation, 50 diffusion steps, 14-layer denoiser, dimensions and attention heads, convolution settings, duration-estimator architecture, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training iterations, and RTX 4090 hardware. It adds a project-page link. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although evaluator details are deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work newly engage NAT-EA and G2P-DDM as closely related gloss-conditioned generators, acknowledging prior temporal-gloss conditioning and positioning local fusion as the distinguishing contribution. This substantially revises the earlier positioning around predominantly sentence-level conditioning, beyond routine citation or bibliography changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, experimental discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around temporal grounding and global versus local fusion. GLOS/TAC terminology becomes SIGNER/LTF throughout. Preliminary and method explanations are reorganized, and dedicated implementation, training-objective, and limitation passages are added.

P2.justification: Figure 2 becomes a three-way conditioning comparison, Figure 3 is reorganized into three stages, and Figure 4 adds face-attention paths. Qualitative panels are revised, and Table 5 plus the jerk-curve Figure 6 are added. Table 4 gains gloss-free/gloss-based grouping, while the document adopts a different page template and relocates figures.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the paper through comparisons with closely related gloss-conditioned methods, concrete implementation settings, smoothness evidence, and an explicit transfer limitation. These improve support for the contribution and reproducibility relative to v1. The gain is limited by removed conditioning controls, undefined ± statistics, and unavailable supplementary evaluator details and cross-evaluator results. The revised scores themselves cannot establish improvement because the method and evaluation settings changed.
